Each topic: id (used by the help icons and banners), title, summary, icon (one of the names in lib/models/tutorial.dart), usedFor, video (title + url; url null = 'coming soon' placeholder), sections (heading + text and/or bullets). General health information only, not medical advice.

topics.title: Measuring your blood pressure
topics.summary: Get a reading you can trust, at home or at a clinic.

video.title: How to measure blood pressure at home

sections.heading: Before you measure
bullets: No coffee, exercise or smoking for 30 minutes before.
Empty your bladder, then sit quietly for 5 minutes.
Sit with your back supported and both feet flat on the floor.
Rest your arm on a table so the cuff is at the level of your heart.
Use a cuff that fits your arm, on bare skin, not over a sleeve.

sections.heading: Taking the reading
bullets: Stay still and do not talk while the machine measures.
Take 2 readings, 1 to 2 minutes apart, and use the average.

sections.heading: Which number to enter
sections.text: A reading looks like 146/90 mmHg. Enter the TOP (first) number, called systolic pressure: 146 in this example.

topics.title: Weight, height and BMI
topics.summary: How to weigh yourself and how the app works out your BMI.

sections.heading: Weight
bullets: Weigh yourself in the morning, after the toilet and before breakfast.
Wear light clothes and no shoes.
Use the same scale each time, on a hard, flat floor.

sections.heading: Height
bullets: Stand straight against a wall, without shoes, heels together.
Look straight ahead; ask someone to mark the top of your head.
Measure from the floor to the mark, in centimetres.

sections.heading: Your BMI
sections.text: You never type your BMI. The app calculates it from your weight and the height saved in My details: BMI = weight (kg) / height (m) x height (m). Example: 70 kg and 1.70 m gives 70 / 2.89 = 24.2.

topics.title: Cholesterol
topics.summary: Where to find your total cholesterol and how to convert the units.

sections.heading: Where to find it
sections.text: Total cholesterol comes from a blood test (a lipid profile) at a clinic or lab. Use the TOTAL cholesterol line of the report, not LDL or HDL.

sections.heading: Converting mmol/L to mg/dL
sections.text: Most Malaysian lab reports use mmol/L, but the app asks for mg/dL. Multiply by 38.67. Example: 6.1 mmol/L x 38.67 = 236 mg/dL.

topics.title: Blood sugar and HbA1c
topics.summary: Fasting blood sugar, glucose and HbA1c: what they are and the units.
topics.usedFor: Fasting Blood Sugar, Blood Glucose, Average Glucose, HbA1c

video.title: How to read a blood sugar test

sections.heading: Fasting blood sugar
sections.text: Your blood sugar after not eating or drinking anything except plain water for at least 8 hours, usually first thing in the morning. It comes from a finger-prick meter or a blood test.

sections.heading: Blood glucose / average glucose
sections.text: A blood sugar reading from your latest test or clinic visit. If you have several, use a typical one, not your highest.

sections.heading: HbA1c
sections.text: A blood test that shows your average blood sugar over the last 2 to 3 months, written as a percentage (for example 6.6%). It is on your lab report; no fasting is needed.

sections.heading: Converting mmol/L to mg/dL
sections.text: Malaysian meters and reports often show mmol/L, but the app asks for mg/dL. Multiply by 18. Example: 7.8 mmol/L x 18 = 140 mg/dL.

topics.title: The exercise stress test
topics.summary: What the treadmill test measures, and where each number is on the report.
topics.usedFor: Max Heart Rate, ST Depression, chest pain during the test

video.title: What happens during a stress test

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: A test at a hospital or heart clinic: you walk on a treadmill that gets faster while an ECG records your heart. Staff watch you the whole time. Only enter results from a real test; if you have not had one, choose 'No' and the app uses a check that does not need it.

sections.heading: The numbers on the report
bullets: Max heart rate: the highest heart rate reached during the test, in beats per minute (bpm).
ST depression: how far a part of the ECG line (the ST segment) dropped during exercise, in millimetres (mm). Your report or doctor gives this number.
Chest pain during the test: whether exercise brought on chest pain (exercise-induced angina).

topics.title: Chest pain type and resting ECG
topics.summary: How to choose the right option for these two heart questions.
topics.usedFor: Chest Pain Type, Resting ECG Result (Heart deep check)

sections.heading: Chest pain type
bullets: Typical angina: pressure or tightness in the chest that comes with effort or stress and goes away with rest.
Atypical angina: chest discomfort with only some of those features.
Non-anginal pain: chest pain that does not seem related to the heart (for example it changes when you press on the chest or move).
No chest pain (asymptomatic): you have no chest pain.

sections.heading: Resting ECG result
sections.text: An ECG taken while you lie still. The result is written on the report: 'normal', an 'ST-T wave abnormality', or 'left ventricular hypertrophy' (LVH). If you are not sure, ask the clinic that did it.

sections.heading: Chest pain right now?
sections.text: Severe chest pain, or pain with sweating or shortness of breath, is an emergency. Call 999 at once; do not use the app.

topics.title: Understanding your results
topics.summary: What the risk percentage means, and what to do next.

sections.heading: The percentage
sections.text: The AI compares your answers with patterns in large health datasets and estimates how likely the disease is for people like you. Roughly, 30% means that about 30 in 100 people with answers like yours have the disease.

sections.heading: The colours
bullets: Green (below 30%): low risk.
Orange (30 to 60%): moderate risk.
Red (above 60%): high risk.

sections.heading: It is not a diagnosis
sections.text: This is a screening estimate. A low result does not mean you are healthy, and a high result does not mean you have the disease. Show your result to a doctor, especially if it is moderate or high.

topics.title: Healthy habits for your heart
topics.summary: Small daily changes that lower the risk of all three diseases.

video.title: Five habits for a healthier heart

sections.heading: Every week
bullets: Be active for at least 150 minutes a week, such as a brisk 30-minute walk on 5 days.
Go for regular health checks: blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol.

sections.heading: Every day
bullets: Eat fruit and vegetables every day: half your plate as vegetables and fruit.
Choose less salt, sugar and fried food.
Do not smoke. Ask your clinic about the mQuit quit-smoking service if you want to stop.
If you drink alcohol, drink less.

topics.title: Spot a stroke: act F.A.S.T.
topics.summary: The four signs of a stroke, and why every minute counts.

sections.heading: F.A.S.T.
bullets: Face: one side of the face droops. Ask them to smile.
Arms: one arm is weak or numb. Ask them to raise both arms.
Speech: speech is slurred or strange. Ask them to repeat a simple sentence.
Time: call 999 at once, and note the time the signs started.

sections.heading: Why speed matters
sections.text: Treatment works best in the first hours. Do not wait to see if the signs go away, and do not drive yourself to hospital.

topics.title: Chronic disease and infections
topics.summary: Why people with heart disease or diabetes should take extra care.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Infections such as COVID-19 and influenza are more likely to become serious in people with heart disease, diabetes or a past stroke.

sections.heading: Simple protection
bullets: Wash your hands often with soap and water.
Ask your clinic which vaccines are recommended for you.
Keep your blood sugar and blood pressure under control.
Stay home and rest when you are unwell.
